contents.text: Argumentative writing is based on claims, evidence, and analysis. Analysis explains how and why the evidence supports the claim.
Strong analysis makes this connection by providing a statement of value, underlying principle, or general interpretive rule that helps readers to understand how the evidence supports the claim.

header.text: A statement of value is a statement about fundamental priorities that can be used to guide decisions.

sentences.text: Claim: Parents should not let their children watch television for more than an hour per day.
Evidence: Children who watch several hours of television per day spend less time outside than they would otherwise.
Analysis: It's vital that children spend time outside.

header.text: An underlying principle is a belief or understanding about how the world works.

sentences.text: Claim: Romeo and Juliet do not really love each other.
Evidence: They claim to be in love after only a few brief conversations.
Analysis: True love requires long periods of time in which two people get to know each other.

header.text: A general interpretive rule is a rule that can be used to interpret a certain type of information.

sentences.text: Claim: Ben Franklin was a social visionary.
Evidence: He was an outspoken opponent of slavery a century before it was legally abolished.
Analysis: The mark of a visionary is the ability to go against prevailing social norms and institutions for the sake of higher principles.

header.text: Analysis should not:

text.text: discuss aspects of the evidence that are unrelated to the claim
jump too quickly to conclusions about "what should be done"
make assumptions or interpretations that are not actually supported by the evidence
